text:
Education in Finland is characterized by a highly equitable, publicly funded, and comprehensive system where municipal governments administer schools from preschool through tertiary education. Compulsory basic education consists of nine years of comprehensive schooling (grades 1–9), known as *peruskoulu* , followed by three to four years of upper secondary education, which is also now compulsory. The system emphasizes small class sizes, minimal homework, and a focus on student well-being and play-based learning in early childhood. Grading is formative rather than punitive, with no high-stakes testing until the end of upper secondary school. A key feature is the requirement for students to learn a second language (typically Finnish or Swedish) alongside English, fostering multilingualism from a young age.
Post-compulsory education bifurcates into academic upper secondary schools (leading to the *ylioppilastutkinto* matriculation exam) and vocational schools, though permeability between the two exists. Tertiary education comprises traditional universities focused on theoretical research and universities of applied sciences focused on industry-oriented skills. Admissions are strictly merit-based, transparent, and objective, relying on grades and standardized exams rather than essays or extracurriculars. While tuition is free for residents of the European Economic Area, non-EEA students face fees since 2017. The system is renowned globally for its high quality, low dropout rates, and successful integration of vocational and academic pathways, serving as a model for educational reform worldwide.
